tips.title: SPICED for exchange rates
tips.body: **S**trong **P**ound, **I**mports **C**heap, **E**xports **D**ear. Backwards it is **WPIDEC**: **W**eak **P**ound, **I**mports **D**ear, **E**xports **C**heap. Work out which way the pound moved first, then apply it. To convert, multiply going **from** pounds and divide coming **back** to them.

tips.title: Tech SPED things up
tips.body: The specification's four technologies spell **SPED**: **S**ocial media, **P**ayment systems, **E**-commerce, **D**igital communication. For each one ask what it changes for the business: its sales, its costs, or one of the four Ps. A business that adopts them early sells further and cheaper; one that ignores them is the threat's first victim.

tips.title: Internal stakeholders are paid by it or own it
tips.body: **Internal**: owners, managers, employees — the people inside the business, paid by it or owning it. **External**: everyone else with a stake — customers, suppliers, the local community, pressure groups and the government. Name the stakeholder, say what they **want**, then say where two of them **conflict**.

tips.title: Name the stakeholder and what they want
tips.body: A stakeholder answer that lists *customers, employees, suppliers* earns little. Say what each one **wants** and where two of them **conflict**: shareholders want dividends, employees want higher pay, and the same profit cannot do both.

tips.title: Interest rates work through borrowing
tips.body: A rate rise makes loans dearer, so businesses invest less and customers with mortgages spend less. Always run the chain through to **this** business rather than stopping at "it is bad for business".

tips.title: Write the rate as a sentence first
tips.body: Put the rate down as **£1 = €1.20** before calculating. Then read the direction you need: going **from pounds**, multiply; going **to pounds**, divide. Writing the line out means the decision is made from the words rather than from a half-remembered rule.

why.matters: A business does not choose the weather it trades in. Interest rates, exchange rates, a new law, a new technology, a pressure group's campaign: none of them asks the owner first, and every one of them reaches the business's sales, its costs or its profit. This topic is about seeing those forces coming and following each one to its effect on **this** business. The exam's favourite question is a chain — this changed outside, so this happens inside — and a business that moves early does better than one that waits.

examples.title: The holiday that got dearer
examples.body:
A hotel in Spain charges **€440** for the week. At **£1 = €1.25** that is **£352**; when the pound weakens to **£1 = €1.10** the same room costs **£400**, and nothing about the hotel has changed.

A clothes shop importing jeans priced in euros is hit exactly the same way: a weaker pound makes imports dearer (**WPIDEC**). The other way round, a strong pound makes imports cheaper and exports dearer to foreign buyers (**SPICED**). To turn euros into pounds, divide by the rate.

props.caption: the same €440 hotel bill, two exchange rates

visual.alt: Two bars in proportion: the same four hundred and forty euro hotel bill costs three hundred and fifty-two pounds at one pound twenty-five and four hundred pounds at one pound ten

examples.title: The mortgage and the sofa shop
examples.body:
When the interest rate rises, a family's monthly mortgage payment goes up, so there is less left over, and a sofa is exactly the purchase that waits. The sofa shop is hit twice: its customers buy less, and its own bank loan costs more each month.

A rate rise is one number changing at the Bank of England, and the chain runs from there to a shop that has done nothing wrong — which is why the exam wants the chain written out, not just "interest rates are bad for business".

visual.alt: A table following a rise in interest rates to a sofa shop: mortgage payments rise so families buy fewer sofas, the shop's own loan repayments rise so its costs go up, and savers earning more are only a small offset

examples.title: The headphones that died in a week
examples.body:
Consumer law says a product must be of **satisfactory quality**, **fit for purpose** and **as described**. Headphones that stop working after a week fail the first test, so the shop must repair, replace or refund, whatever its sign says.

Meeting the law costs the business money — replacement stock, staff time, better suppliers — and breaking it costs more: refunds anyway, fines, and customers who tell everyone. Legislation is a cost either way; the business only chooses which.

visual.alt: A table of consumer law's three tests, satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described, applied to a pair of headphones that stopped working after a week and so fail the first

steps.title: Who has a stake in a business
steps.body:
A **stakeholder** is anyone with an interest in what a business does, because they are affected by it or can affect it. The specification lists eight:

- **Owners or shareholders**: want profit and a return on their investment.
- **Employees**: want fair pay, job security, safe conditions.
- **Managers**: want the business to hit its targets, and their own bonuses.
- **Customers**: want quality, value and good service.
- **Suppliers**: want regular orders and prompt payment.
- **The local community**: wants jobs, and not noise, traffic or pollution.
- **Pressure groups**: campaign on one issue, such as the environment or animal welfare.
- **The government**: wants tax revenue, jobs, and the law obeyed.

The first three are **internal**, inside the business. The rest are **external**.

visuals.alt: A table of the eight stakeholder groups, whether each is internal or external, and what each wants

check.prompt: Which stakeholder mainly wants regular orders and to be paid on time?
check.solution: Suppliers sell to the business, so their interest is in a steady flow of orders and prompt payment for them.

options: Customers
The government
Employees
Suppliers

steps.title: Stakeholders pull in different directions
steps.body:
Stakeholders want different things, and a decision that pleases one often costs another. That is **stakeholder conflict**, and it is the heart of most 9 and 12 mark questions on this section.

- Owners want higher profit; employees want higher pay. The same pound cannot go to both.
- Customers want lower prices; suppliers want higher prices for what they sell to the business.
- Owners want a new factory; the local community wants no traffic and no noise.
- Managers want to cut costs by automating; employees want their jobs.

Stakeholders also **influence** the business, not just react to it. Customers can stop buying. Employees can leave, or strike. Suppliers can refuse credit. Pressure groups can generate bad publicity. The government can fine or close a business that breaks the law.

In an exam, name the stakeholders in the case, say what each wants, show where they clash, and then judge which the business should put first and why.

visuals.problem: A supermarket wants to open 24 hours

steps.text: Owners: more sales and profit from night-time customers
Employees: some want the extra hours; others do not want night shifts
Local residents: lorries and car doors at 3 a.m.
The judgement: go ahead if the extra profit outweighs the cost of unhappy staff and neighbours, and if the noise can be managed
steps.note: Name who wins, who loses, and what tips it

check.prompt: A business cuts its prices to win customers. Which stakeholder is most likely to be unhappy as a direct result?
check.solution: Lower prices help customers and may raise sales, but each sale earns less, so unless volume rises a lot the owners' profit falls. Customers gain; owners carry the risk.

markScheme.description: the owners

options: The government, because prices are lower
Pressure groups, because prices are lower
The owners, because profit per sale falls
Customers, because they pay less

steps.title: Technology: four kinds, and what they change
steps.body:
The specification names four types of technology:

- **E-commerce**: selling online through a website or app.
- **Social media**: promoting to customers and talking with them, at almost no cost.
- **Digital communication**: email, video calls, messaging, between staff and with customers and suppliers.
- **Payment systems**: card, contactless, phone and online payments.

What they change:

- **Sales**: a website sells to the whole country, 24 hours a day, so revenue can rise far beyond what one shop could take.
- **Costs**: some fall, because there is less need for premises, print advertising and paper; others rise, because websites, delivery and IT have to be paid for.
- **The marketing mix**: place moves online, promotion moves to social media, price faces online comparison, and the product can change in response to reviews and data.

Technology is also a **threat**: competitors use it too, and a business that does not keep up loses customers to one that does.

visuals.alt: Four boxes for e-commerce, social media, digital communication and payment systems around the word technology

check.prompt: A café starts accepting contactless payments. Which type of technology is this?
check.solution: Contactless is a payment system. It speeds up service and reduces cash handling, at the cost of a small fee on each transaction.

markScheme.description: payment systems

options: Payment systems
E-commerce
Social media
Digital communication

steps.title: Legislation: the two laws that matter
steps.body:
Businesses must obey the law, and the specification focuses on two areas.

**Consumer law** protects customers. Goods must be of **satisfactory quality**, **fit for purpose** and **as described**, and customers have rights to a refund, repair or replacement if they are not. Adverts must not mislead.

**Employment law** protects workers. It covers **recruitment** (no discrimination in who is hired), **pay** (the national minimum wage and living wage), **discrimination** (equal treatment regardless of sex, race, age, disability and so on), and **health and safety** (a safe workplace, training, protective equipment).

Why the law matters to the business:

- **Cost of meeting it**: minimum wages, safety equipment, staff training, replacing faulty goods.
- **Consequences of breaking it**: fines, compensation claims, being closed down, bad publicity, and losing customers who no longer trust the business.

Meeting the law costs money. Breaking it usually costs more.

rows: quality, fit for purpose, as described
props.title: Legislation on the specification

visuals.alt: A table of consumer law and employment law, what each covers, and the consequence of breaking it

check.prompt: A shop refuses to refund a customer for a kettle that stopped working after a week. Which principle of consumer law has it ignored?
check.solution: A kettle that fails in a week is not of satisfactory quality, and the customer has the right to a refund, repair or replacement. The other three are employment law.

steps.title: The economy: six things that move
steps.body:
The **economic climate** is the state of the economy as a whole, and a business has no control over it. Six measures matter:

- **Unemployment**: when it rises, people have less to spend, so demand falls; but recruiting is easier and wages are held down.
- **Consumer income**: when incomes rise, people buy more, especially luxuries; when they fall, they trade down to cheaper products.
- **Inflation**: rising prices push up a business's costs, and shrink what customers' pay can buy.
- **Interest rates**: the cost of borrowing. Higher rates make loans dearer for the business, and leave customers with mortgages less to spend.
- **Taxation**: VAT raises prices to customers; corporation tax takes a share of profit; income tax reduces what customers have left to spend.
- **Exchange rates**: the price of the pound in other currencies. It changes the cost of imports and the price of exports.

The skill is to take the measure the case mentions and follow the chain to the business's sales, costs or profit.

rows: higher costs, pressure to raise prices
props.title: When each measure rises

visuals.alt: A table of the six economic measures and the effect of a rise in each on a typical business

steps.title: Exchange rates: SPICED
steps.body:
The exchange rate is how much foreign currency one pound buys: £1 = €1.20 means a pound is worth 1.20 euros.

To turn pounds into euros, **multiply** by the rate. To turn euros into pounds, **divide**.

When the pound gets **stronger** (buys more euros), imports get cheaper for UK businesses and UK exports get dearer for foreign customers. The mnemonic is **SPICED**: **S**trong **P**ound, **I**mports **C**heaper, **E**xports **D**earer. A weak pound does the opposite.

Which matters depends on the business. An importer likes a strong pound. An exporter likes a weak one. A business that does both is partly protected.

visuals.problem: A UK shop imports bikes at €600 each

steps.text: The pound strengthens to £1 = €1.50: cost $= 600 \div 1.50 = £400$
Each bike costs the shop £100 less: it can cut its price or keep a bigger margin
Had the pound weakened to €1.00, the bike would cost £600, and the shop would have to raise its price or lose margin

check.prompt: A UK business imports goods costing \$900. The exchange rate is £1 = \$1.80. What is the cost in pounds?
check.solution: Dollars to pounds: divide by the rate. $900 \div 1.80 = £500$.

steps.title: How a business responds
steps.body:
External influences cannot be controlled, but they can be **responded to**, and the last part of the specification is about that.

**To a change in technology**: adopt it. Sell online, promote on social media, take new payment types, before competitors make it the norm.

**To a change in legislation**: comply, and build the cost in. Train staff, adjust prices if costs rise, and use compliance as a selling point: customers trust a business that treats them and its staff properly.

**To a change in the economic climate**: adjust the mix. In a downturn, cut prices or offer cheaper ranges, cut costs that customers do not notice, and look for customers whose spending holds up. When incomes rise, move up-market. When the pound moves, an importer or exporter can change prices, change suppliers, or agree prices in advance.

The common thread: a business that watches its environment and moves early does better than one that waits to be hit.

visuals.problem: A garden centre and a bad year

steps.text: The economy: a recession cuts customers' income. Response: a cheaper plant range and more offers
Technology: a rival launches online ordering. Response: its own website with local delivery
Legislation: the minimum wage rises. Response: fewer seasonal staff, more self-service tills
Each response takes an external change and turns it into a decision the business can make
steps.note: The chain always ends in what the business does about it

check.prompt: Consumer incomes fall during a recession. Which response by a restaurant is most likely to protect its sales?
check.solution: When customers have less to spend, a cheaper option keeps them coming. Raising prices or moving up-market does the opposite, and cutting all promotion makes it harder to attract the customers who remain.

steps.title: Your turn: read the case for its external influences
steps.body:
A Section B case study never labels its external influences. It buries them in the story, and the skill is to spot them.

**Case:** Sunita runs a small business importing hand-woven rugs from India and selling them through her shop and website. This year the pound has weakened against the rupee, a large online homeware retailer has started selling similar rugs with free delivery, and a new law requires clearer labelling of imported textiles.

Before the check, find the three external influences and decide which part of the specification each belongs to.

steps.text: The pound has weakened: the economy, exchange rates. Her import costs rise
A large online rival with free delivery: technology, e-commerce. Pressure on her price and place
A new labelling law: legislation. A compliance cost, and a possible fine if ignored
Three influences, three chains, each ending in Sunita's costs, sales or profit
steps.note: That is the structure of the 6 marker that follows

check.prompt: Which of the three external influences raises the cost in pounds of every rug Sunita buys from her Indian supplier?
check.skill: spotting external influences in a case
check.solution: A weaker pound buys fewer rupees, so each rug costs Sunita more pounds. The rival affects her sales and prices; the labelling law adds a cost, but to her own packaging, not to what the supplier charges.

markScheme.description: the weaker pound

options: The online rival
The labelling law
None of them
The weaker pound

steps.title: Going deeper: chains that end in the business, and judgements that name the condition
steps.body:
Three habits separate the top answers on this section.

**Follow the chain to the business.** *Interest rates rise* is not a point. *Interest rates rise, so Jamal's loan repayments increase, so his costs rise while his sales are falling, so his profit is squeezed from both sides* is a point. Every chain ends in sales, costs, profit, cash or reputation, for the business in the case.

**Show that stakeholders conflict, then choose.** A 9 marker on Sunday opening wants the owners' profit against the employees' weekends against the neighbours' sleep, and then a decision with the deciding factor named: whether the noise can be solved, whether the extra profit is large, whether staff can be found who want the hours.

**Say what it depends on.** A 12 marker on whether technology is a benefit or a threat ends with the condition: *it depends on whether the business uses the technology or only suffers it*, and then how the answer would change if that condition were different. The examiner is looking for that sentence.

And the exchange-rate question: know which way to divide, and know SPICED. It is the one place in this section where a wrong number costs a certain mark.

rows: costs up, margin down or price up
sales down unless it competes online
compliance cost, or fine if ignored
loan costs up, customer spending down

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Stakeholders**: owners, employees, managers (internal); customers, suppliers, community, pressure groups, government (external). Each wants something different, and they **conflict**; a good answer names the conflict and judges it.
- **Technology**: e-commerce, social media, digital communication, payment systems. Changes sales, costs and the marketing mix, and is a threat to a business that ignores it.
- **Consumer law**: satisfactory quality, fit for purpose, as described. **Employment law**: recruitment, pay, discrimination, health and safety.
- **Legislation** costs money to meet and more to break: fines, claims, closure, lost trust.
- **The economy**: unemployment, consumer income, inflation, interest rates, taxation, exchange rates. Follow the one in the case to the business's sales, costs or profit.
- **Exchange rates**: divide foreign currency by the rate to get pounds. **SPICED**: strong pound, imports cheaper, exports dearer.
- **Responses**: adopt technology, comply and build the cost in, adjust prices and costs to the economy. A business that moves early does better than one that waits.

questions.solution: Pounds $=$ dollars $\div$ the rate: $12\,000 \div 1.5 = £8000$. The rate says how many dollars one pound buys, so dividing turns dollars into pounds.

questions.solution: Point plus development. Its loan repayments rise, which means it has less money left for other spending, so its profit falls.

questions.solution: A stronger pound means each euro buys fewer pounds, so a French shop needs more euros to pay the same price in pounds. The jam is dearer in France and sales there fall. Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer.

Its jam becomes cheaper in France, so it sells more there

questions.prompt: A UK clothing retailer imports jeans at €40 each. Last year the exchange rate was £1 = €1.25; this year it is £1 = €1.10. Calculate how much more, in pounds, each pair of jeans costs the retailer this year.
questions.solution: Last year: $40 \div 1.25 = £32$. This year: $40 \div 1.10 = £36.36$. The increase is $36.36 - 32 = £4.36$ per pair. The pound has weakened, so imports cost more; the retailer has to raise its price or accept a smaller profit margin.

markScheme.description: difference of the two

questions.prompt: A small furniture maker has taken on three staff for the first time. Analyse the impact on the business of having to comply with employment law.
questions.solution: Two chains. Costs: it must pay at least the minimum wage, provide a safe workshop, and follow rules on hours and holidays, so its wage and equipment costs rise, which reduces the profit on each piece of furniture unless prices rise. Benefits: fair pay and safe conditions mean staff stay and work well, so the business avoids the cost of recruiting again and keeps its reputation, and it avoids fines and compensation claims that could close a small business.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Cost impact identified: minimum wage, safety equipment, holiday pay, applied to a small maker taking on staff
Developed to an outcome: higher costs, lower margin, or prices raised
Benefit or risk identified: motivated staff who stay, or the fines and claims avoided
Developed to an outcome: lower recruitment costs and a protected reputation, or the business kept trading

questions.modelAnswer: Employment law raises the furniture maker's costs. It must pay each of the three staff at least the minimum wage, give them paid holiday, and make the workshop safe, which means buying guards for machinery and protective equipment, so its costs rise and the profit on each piece falls unless it can raise prices. On the other hand, meeting the law protects the business. Staff who are paid fairly and work safely are more likely to stay and work well, which saves the cost and disruption of recruiting again, and the business avoids fines or a compensation claim from an injured worker, either of which could close a business this small. So the law adds cost, but breaking it would cost far more.

questions.prompt: Jamal owns a café near a large factory. The factory has announced it will close next year, and interest rates have just risen. Analyse the impact of these changes in the economic climate on Jamal's café.
questions.solution: Two chains rooted in the case. Unemployment: the factory's workers are the café's lunchtime customers, so when it closes they have no income to spend and the café's sales fall sharply, so Jamal may have to cut staff or hours. Interest rates: if Jamal has a loan, his repayments rise, so costs go up just as sales fall; and customers with mortgages have less to spend, so demand drops further. A grade 9 answer notes the two effects arrive together and reinforce each other.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: Unemployment from the closure identified and applied to the café's customers
Developed to an outcome: lunchtime sales fall, so revenue and profit drop, so hours or staff are cut
Interest rate rise identified and applied to Jamal's loan or his customers' spending
Developed to an outcome: higher costs, lower demand, or both at once

questions.modelAnswer: The factory closing will raise local unemployment, and the factory's workers are Jamal's lunchtime customers. Once they lose their income they will stop buying lunches, so the café's sales fall sharply, which means Jamal may have to cut opening hours or staff to keep the business afloat. The rise in interest rates makes this worse. If Jamal has a bank loan for the café his repayments increase, so his costs go up at the same time as his sales come down, squeezing profit from both sides. His remaining customers with mortgages will also have less to spend, so demand falls further. The two changes reinforce each other, which is why Jamal needs to respond quickly, perhaps by finding new customers such as nearby offices or by offering cheaper options.

questions.prompt: A bakery's owners want to open on Sundays to increase profit. Its employees do not want to work Sundays, and residents living nearby have complained about early-morning delivery noise. Justify whether the owners should go ahead.
questions.solution: Choose, argue both ways, name the deciding factor. For opening: more revenue and profit for the owners, more hours for any staff who want them. Against: employees may leave, so recruitment costs and lost skills; residents could complain to the council, which could restrict the bakery's hours altogether. Judgement: it depends on whether the extra profit outweighs the risk of losing staff and goodwill, and on whether the noise can be solved, for example by later deliveries on Sundays.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 3): limited points, little application, no real judgement
Level 2 (4 to 6): developed reasoning for the choice with some application; a judgement is made
Level 3 (7 to 9): developed reasoning for the choice and against the alternative, applied throughout, with a justified judgement that names the deciding factor

criteria.text: A clear decision with developed reasons, applied to the bakery's profit, staff or neighbours
Developed reasons on the other side, applied to the case
A judgement naming the deciding factor: the size of the extra profit, the risk of losing staff, or whether the noise can be solved

questions.modelAnswer: The owners should go ahead, but only if they can meet the other stakeholders part of the way. Opening on Sundays would increase revenue, and the bakery's fixed costs such as rent are already paid, so most of the extra sales would be profit, which is the owners' main objective. However, the employees are the stakeholders who make it work: if they are forced to work Sundays some may leave, and replacing skilled bakers costs money and time, so the extra profit could disappear into recruitment. The residents matter too, because complaints to the council could lead to restrictions on the bakery's hours every day, not just Sunday. The deciding factor is whether the conflicts can be managed: paying a higher Sunday rate so that staff volunteer, and moving Sunday deliveries later in the morning. If the owners can do both, the extra profit is worth having; if they cannot, the damage to staff and neighbours outweighs it.

questions.prompt: Evaluate whether technology is more of a benefit or a threat to a small independent bookshop.
questions.solution: Both sides, applied, then it depends on. Threat: online retailers sell the same books cheaper with next-day delivery, so customers leave; e-books remove the need for a shop at all. Benefit: the shop can sell online itself, use social media to reach readers cheaply, take card and phone payments, run a loyalty database, and host events promoted online. Judgement: it depends on whether the bookshop uses technology or only suffers it, and on whether its customers value the experience a shop gives; for a shop that competes on price alone technology is a threat, for one that competes on service it is a tool.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 4): some knowledge with little business terminology, limited application to the business, few connections between points, and a conclusion resting on generic assertions

Level 2 (5 to 8): mostly accurate knowledge with terminology in places, sound application to the business though not always consistent, chains of reasoning that connect points, and a conclusion based on sound evaluation

Level 3 (9 to 12): accurate knowledge and terminology throughout, detailed application to the business throughout, detailed interconnected points with logical chains of reasoning, and a valid, well-reasoned conclusion

criteria.text: Reaches level 1: some accurate knowledge, applied at least a little, with a conclusion of some kind
Reaches level 2: sound application to this business, with chains of reasoning and a supported conclusion
Reaches level 3: accurate and detailed throughout, with logical chains and a well-reasoned conclusion

questions.modelAnswer: Technology is a serious threat to a small bookshop. Large online retailers sell the same titles more cheaply and deliver them the next day, so customers who care mainly about price and convenience have little reason to visit, and e-books remove the need for a physical book at all, so the shop's sales fall. Yet the same technology gives the shop tools it never had. It can sell online through its own website and reach readers beyond its town; it can promote new titles and events on social media for almost nothing, which a small shop could never afford in print advertising; card and phone payments make buying easy; and a customer database lets it tell regulars when an author they like has a new book. Whether technology is a benefit or a threat therefore depends on how the bookshop uses it and on what it competes on. A shop that tries to compete with online retailers on price will lose, and technology is the reason. A shop that competes on knowledge, events and personal recommendation, and uses technology to reach and keep those customers, will find it is a benefit. For most independent bookshops the second is the only strategy that works, so technology is a benefit to the ones that survive and a threat to the ones that ignore it.

questions.prompt: A UK toy importer buys from China and sells only in the UK. The pound weakens against the Chinese currency. Which is correct?
questions.skill: exchange rates applied to an importer
questions.solution: A weaker pound buys less foreign currency, so the same order of toys costs more pounds. The importer's costs rise, and because it sells only in the UK there is no export gain to offset it. Weak Pound: Imports Dearer, Exports Cheaper, and this business only imports.

markScheme.description: costs rise, prices up or profit down

options: Its costs rise, so it must raise prices or accept lower profit
Nothing changes, because it buys and sells in pounds throughout
Its sales abroad rise, because a weak pound makes exports cheaper
Its costs fall, so it can cut its prices and sell more toys

questions.prompt: The government raises VAT. Which business is most likely to be worst affected?
questions.solution: VAT is added to the price customers pay in the UK. A restaurant must either raise its prices, losing price-sensitive customers, or absorb the tax and cut its margin. VAT is not charged on exports, so the exporter is barely touched, and the other two options are not defined by VAT at all.

markScheme.description: the price-sensitive restaurant

options: A business with no employees
A charity
A restaurant whose customers are sensitive to price
A firm that exports all its output

questions.prompt: A small hotel has seen bookings fall during a recession. Analyse two ways the hotel could respond to the change in the economic climate.
questions.solution: Two developed responses. Price: offer cheaper rooms or mid-week deals, so customers with less income can still afford a stay, so occupancy rises even if revenue per room falls. Costs: cut spending that does not affect guests, such as renegotiating with suppliers or reducing staff hours in quiet periods, so the hotel stays profitable at lower occupancy. Or: target a different market, such as business travellers or staycations, whose spending holds up better.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2): points made with limited development, little link to the case
Level 2 (3 to 4): one developed chain, applied to the business
Level 3 (5 to 6): two developed chains of reasoning, each applied to the business and reaching an outcome

criteria.text: A response identified and applied to a hotel in a recession: lower prices, special offers, cost cutting, or a new market
Developed to an outcome: higher occupancy, protected profit, or revenue from a new segment
A second, different response identified and applied
Developed to an outcome

questions.modelAnswer: The hotel could reduce its prices, for example with mid-week deals or a lower rate for longer stays. In a recession customers have less income, so a cheaper room makes a stay affordable again, which raises occupancy; a room sold cheaply still earns more than an empty room, so revenue is higher than it would otherwise be. It could also cut costs that guests do not notice. Renegotiating with laundry and food suppliers, or reducing staff hours on quiet days, lowers the hotel's costs, which means it can stay profitable even with fewer bookings. Together the two responses attack the problem from both sides: more bookings at a lower price, and lower costs to serve them.

questions.prompt: A UK business sells a product for £20 in France. The exchange rate moves from £1 = €1.25 to £1 = €1.10. Calculate by how many euros the French price falls.
questions.solution: Going **from** pounds, multiply. At £1 = €1.25 the price is $20 \times 1.25 = €25$; at £1 = €1.10 it is $20 \times 1.10 = €22$. The price falls by $25 - 22 = €3$. A weaker pound makes exports cheaper: WPIDEC.

markScheme.description: both prices found

questions.prompt: Which of these is an internal stakeholder of a business?
questions.solution: **Internal** stakeholders are inside the business: owners, managers and employees. Suppliers, customers, the community, pressure groups and the government are **external**.

markScheme.description: an employee

options: A supplier
The local community
An employee
The government

questions.prompt: State the term for the percentage a bank charges a business each year for borrowing money.
questions.solution: The **interest rate**. When it rises, a business with a loan pays more each month, and customers with mortgages have less left to spend.

markScheme.description: interest rate

questions.prompt: A new law raises the minimum wage. Which business is most directly affected?
questions.solution: Employment law reaches a business through its **pay bill**. The café pays the minimum wage to twelve people, so its costs rise at once; the others either have no employees or already pay above the new minimum.

markScheme.description: the café with staff on the minimum wage

options: A café employing twelve part-time staff on the minimum wage
A sole trader working alone from home
A software company paying high salaries
An online shop with no employees

questions.prompt: Interest rates rise from 2% to 5%. A furniture shop has a £50 000 bank loan, and most of its customers buy on credit. Which effect is most likely?
questions.solution: The rate rise reaches the shop twice: its own **repayments** rise, adding to costs, and its customers' **credit** costs more, so fewer buy a sofa on finance and revenue falls. A chain that ends in the business is what the question wants.

markScheme.description: costs up and sales down

options: Its loan becomes cheaper, so profit rises
Customers save less, so they spend more in the shop
Nothing changes, because interest rates only affect banks
Loan repayments rise and fewer customers can afford credit, so profit falls twice

examTechnique.body:
Section 1.5 is where Paper 1 gets its case studies about things happening *to* a business: a rival going online, a new law, a recession, a stakeholder row. The theory is a list of terms, and the multiple choice tests them exactly: which stakeholder is internal, which law covers a faulty kettle, which way the pound moves imports. Learn the six economic measures and the four technologies as lists.

The long questions are won by chains. Take the influence the case names, apply it to *that* business, and follow it to sales, costs, profit, cash or reputation. Stakeholder questions want the conflict shown and then judged. The exchange-rate calculation is the one place a slip costs a certain mark: divide foreign currency by the rate to get pounds, and SPICED for the direction.
examinerErrors: Listing stakeholders without saying what each one wants, or without showing where two of them conflict.
Multiplying instead of dividing in an exchange-rate conversion. £1 = €1.20 means €600 is £500, not £720.
Getting SPICED backwards: a strong pound makes imports cheaper and exports dearer, not the other way round.
Saying a rise in interest rates only affects the business's own loans, and missing that customers with mortgages have less to spend.
Treating unemployment as purely bad for a business. Demand falls, but recruiting becomes easier and wage pressure eases; a grade 9 answer knows both.
Chains that stop at the influence. "Inflation raises costs" is a start, not an answer; it has to reach the business's profit or price.
Answers about businesses in general. If the case is a café, the word café should appear in every paragraph.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer reads the case for its external influences before writing, names which part of the specification each belongs to, and follows each one through a chain that ends in the case business's sales, costs, profit or reputation. On stakeholders it sets out who wants what, shows the conflict, and then decides, naming the factor that tips it. On the economy it knows the second-order effects: interest rates through customers' mortgages as well as the firm's loans, unemployment as easier recruiting as well as lower demand. Its exchange-rate arithmetic is right and it knows which businesses gain from a strong pound and which from a weak one. Its 12 markers end with it depends on, the condition named, and how the answer would change.
